analysis:
Integration of all 21 units: no concrete security regression was found. The functional change is small. NemotronSuperServingPolicy.maximumEncodedBodyBytes goes from 8 MiB to 40 MiB (head ~line 369). NemotronSuperLocalImageBinding.swift adds Failure.bodyTooLarge and splits the encodedHeaderQuote guard (head ~222-226). NemotronSuperLocalImageHTTP.swift maps bodyTooLarge to MediaIngest.MediaError.mediaTooLarge (head 178-179). The rest is docs, changelog and test updates.

Availability and DoS (TB-007, TB-002; T-010/T-029 class): the ingress quote is bodyBytes*32 + templateBytes*4 + 16 MiB, now about 1.28 GiB at the cap. It is reserved on the shared ledger before JSON/base64 parsing or decode. A failed reservation fails closed (Failure.capacity, 503). Other limits are unchanged: one media request per owner (429 otherwise), reservation release in settle, and the size check before any reservation. The transports (localInferenceMaxUploadBytes, CoordinatorClient.maxInboundMessageBytes) are stated to be 32 MiB, below the new 40 MiB bound, so the effective admitted body is unchanged in practice. The tests (bodyBoundHoldsOneSharedIngestPart) assert this relationship. Larger worst-case media charges and smaller default prefix banks are conservative and do not widen T-041 (cache scope, HMAC names and TTL are untouched). The new error string is static and carries no prompt or media content, so there is no A-001 leak. T-050 (temp-file plaintext) is untouched.

Unverified or out of evidence (74 source units were omitted from the replay):
- The transport limit values themselves.
- How the downstream layers translate mediaTooLarge into a status code. Docs say 413 from the chat route, while the unit tests assert 400 for the provider path. This is a correctness or contract question rather than a security one.
- Whether other Failure switches handle bodyTooLarge.
- That the 40 MiB bound is never reachable beyond the 32 MiB transport caps.

No threat-model updates are needed beyond the existing T-041 and TB-007 coverage.
